items.t: Nvidia shares fall as investigation opens into reports CEO was targeted by Chinese intelligence
items.s: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation after reports that chief executive Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, a claim China denies. Shares fell in premarket trading as the story spread.
p: Nvidia said it was launching an independent investigation following reports that its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been the target of “a foreign intelligence effort”. According to the reports, that effort led to a romantic relationship between Huang and a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, who had allegedly been recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Huang has admitted an affair. In a statement he said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family. He also said he was “fully committed to Nvidia” and would work to earn back employees’ confidence. China has denied the spying claims.

Alice Huang reportedly worked for Megaspeed, a datacentre company based in Singapore. Megaspeed has been suspected of routing Nvidia chips to China and evading export controls, though the reporting cited in the evidence does not establish that as fact. Jensen Huang has publicly criticised US export controls on advanced chips, arguing in May 2025 that they had been a failure.

The Financial Times reported that Alice Huang and a business partner, Kang Wei, sought investment in early 2025 for a south-east Asian data centre project worth several hundred million dollars. According to two investors, the pair said they had “no problem securing GPUs” and cited Alibaba as a client. A US hedge fund had claimed six months earlier that Alibaba secretly funded Megaspeed.

Markets reacted quickly. Nvidia ended last week worth $4.5tn, and shares were down around 6% in premarket trading, with more than $200bn potentially wiped from its value once Wall Street opened. Asian markets were recovering, with Japan’s Nikkei up 2.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX up almost 5%. Elon Musk publicly backed a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that criticised Huang’s conduct.

Separately, Bloomberg reported that Alphabet is rolling out a broader range of its tensor processing units, custom chips used to develop and run software, which adds to competitive pressure on Nvidia. Prediction market Polymarket put the chance of Huang resigning or being removed by the end of the year at 15%.
items.cav: The espionage link rests on reports and claims, not on any confirmed finding, and the investigation’s outcome is not yet known. The Alibaba funding claim comes from a hedge fund’s allegation made months earlier, and the investor accounts are second-hand. Market figures are premarket and may change.
items.op: Whatever the facts of this affair, the public interest is in an independent inquiry that is transparent about its findings. Nvidia’s investors and the wider public deserve clear answers on export controls and on who was able to reach its chief executive. Speculation should not substitute for evidence.

items.t: Cop31 opens in Antalya as UN warns heat is building faster and the US stays away
items.s: Climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, opened as the World Meteorological Organization reported that heat is building up in Earth's systems at a faster pace. The United States, which has withdrawn from the international climate framework, will again send no official delegation.
p: The UN’s weather agency said the gap between the energy Earth receives from the sun and the energy it sends back has reached its largest level since measurements began. Releasing its global climate update as the summit got under way, it said 2026 was on course to rank among the four hottest years ever recorded.

According to the agency, average surface temperatures from January to September 2026 ran about 1.47C above the preindustrial level. Monthly sea surface temperature records were broken, and sea levels stood at their highest since record-keeping started. Oceans take in roughly 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and 2026 is on track to be the tenth straight year of record ocean heat.

The agency warned that this heat build-up will intensify extreme weather, including heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the world had moved into an era of severe climate extremes, pointing to a strong El Niño event layered on top of human-caused warming. He added that the people who have done least to cause the problem are suffering most.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister, is presiding over the negotiations in Antalya. Our colleague Adam Morton questioned him about the apparent contradictions in Australia’s record: a country with high emissions is leading the talks while still exporting fossil fuels and approving projects that add pollution.

Young activists at the summit also made their case. Janiely Truká, an Indigenous activist and poet from Brazil who advises Unicef Brazil on youth issues, said that for Indigenous communities the climate crisis threatens their way of life, their traditional knowledge and their future generations. She called for firm funding commitments, protection of Indigenous territories and easier access for young people to these negotiations.

The United States will again have no official government presence at the summit, the second year running. A White House official said the administration would not send anyone and criticised the summit for ignoring what it sees as the damage done by extreme climate policies. About 20 members of Congress travelling to Antalya have been refused the usual State Department support and are relying on philanthropic money. Democratic congressman Sean Casten, who is attending, described the situation as outrageous.

A recent UN report found that the US was the one major economy that did not cut or slow its carbon pollution last year, adding an extra 133m tons of planet-warming gases from coal, oil and gas. President Donald Trump has previously dismissed climate action as a scam. Finance is expected to be the most contentious issue, with developing countries pressing for money that wealthier nations would rather keep off the agenda.
items.cav: The temperature and ocean figures come from a World Meteorological Organization update covering only January to September, so they are provisional. Several claims about the US and the summit come from live coverage and from quotes given by officials and lawmakers, and the sources do not independently verify them. The article does not say what outcomes the talks are likely to produce.
items.op: Transparency at these summits matters as much as ambition. Delegates should publish agendas and funding arrangements early, and governments that talk about climate finance should show the money. Vague promises from any capital, including the host, will not protect the people already paying the price.

items.t: Kraków shooting: Polish prosecutors widen probe as attacker dies in hospital
items.s: Six people were killed when a gunman opened fire in Kraków’s main square over the weekend, and the 24-year-old Polish attacker has since died in hospital. Authorities say the investigation will continue to determine whether he acted alone.
p: Polish investigators opened a terrorism case after a gunman from Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town in southeastern Poland, fired on people in the city’s central square on Saturday afternoon, according to the Guardian’s live coverage. Six people lost their lives, one of them a Briton, and 17 others were wounded. Authorities later said the assailant, who had been hit during an exchange of fire with officers, died in hospital.

A national day of mourning was declared for the first of two planned days. Police said the bodies of three relatives were found at the attacker’s home: his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his 21-year-old sister. Among the wounded were nationals of Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia, as well as two police officers, one of them in serious condition.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect had been drawn to far-right ideas and held “very radical” views. Those remarks were later softened, and nationalist opposition figures challenged the basis on which they had been made. Government spokesperson Adam Szlapka urged restraint in commenting while the initial signs remained unconfirmed.

According to interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka, Poland’s cybercrime bureau, CBZC, has detained five people over online posts praising the shooter. She warned that officers were on heightened alert for possible copycat attacks.

Justice minister Waldemar Zurek said the probe would proceed despite the attacker’s death, with a focus on whether the gunman worked alone. The square reopened on Sunday evening after the security cordon was removed.
items.cav: The account comes from a live blog that relays official statements and has not been independently verified. The interior minister’s ideological claims were partly walked back and their basis has been disputed, so the suspect’s motive remains unclear. The sources do not say what the five detained people are suspected of or whether the posts led to charges.
items.op: A rare mass shooting in a city centre demands facts, not early labels. Poland’s government was right to pull back from a motive it could not yet support. Transparency now means publishing what the investigation establishes, including whether anyone helped the gunman, and treating the detained suspects with the presumption of innocence.

items.t: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admits affair as reports link his companion to alleged Chinese spying
items.s: Nvidia's chief executive has admitted an extramarital affair after US media reports said the woman involved was suspected of spying for Beijing. The company has opened an independent investigation.
p: Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the chipmaker Nvidia, has acknowledged an extramarital affair. On Sunday he said he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologised for the hurt caused to her and their children. He also said he would cooperate with an internal security investigation.

The affair is with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman who is not related to him. According to a New York Times report, which the BBC cites, US intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by China’s top intelligence agency and was spying for Beijing. Her current whereabouts are unknown. She did not respond to a request for comment from the newspaper.

Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm that had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia says it investigated those concerns and found them to be unfounded. The BBC understands that Megaspeed is now under investigation by the Singapore government over earlier claims that it evaded US sanctions on exports of Nvidia’s high-end chips.

The New York Times reported that surveillance captured communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was later identified as Jensen Huang. It remains unclear what intelligence, if any, she gathered and passed on. Nvidia told the BBC it was not aware of any intelligence concerns, and said it trusted the US government would have warned it of a genuine threat. China has rejected the allegations as “groundless”.

The reports have a political dimension. According to the New York Times, Donald Trump was briefed last year on intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was spying for China. Asked whether he wished he had acted on it, Trump said he did not think so and called Huang “an honourable guy”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment, though the newspaper reported that he had overseen a memo last spring warning the administration about the relationship.

The stakes are high because Nvidia sits at the centre of the contest between the US and China over the most advanced technology. Export controls introduced since 2022 have largely shut the company out of the Chinese market, and Huang has pursued talks between Washington and Beijing in an effort to win back access. The affair, the reports suggest, may have complicated his hopes of a broader approval to sell more advanced chips to China.
Huang, born in Taiwan in 1963, co-founded Nvidia after working at AMD. Bloomberg’s billionaires index estimates his fortune at $155bn.
items.cav: Much of the espionage detail is second-hand, drawn from a New York Times report that the BBC relayed, and Alice Huang has not commented. What intelligence she may have passed to Beijing is unknown, and Nvidia’s claim that US national security was not compromised has not been independently verified.
items.op: The question is not Huang’s marriage but whether a company central to national security was kept properly informed. Officials who held intelligence about his associate owe lawmakers and the public a clearer account of what was known and what was done. Reassurance from either Nvidia or the administration is no substitute for transparency.

items.t: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about offering Dana White the press secretary job
items.s: President Donald Trump has said he was not serious when he publicly offered the White House press secretary job to Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. The offer had been announced a day earlier.
p: On Sunday, Trump told reporters he had been joking when he announced the offer, according to the BBC. He said White liked the idea but described the invitation as lighthearted.

The offer had been made in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, in which Trump urged White to take the role and predicted he would be unlike any previous press secretary. Trump also said White could bring several current and former mixed martial arts fighters along as aides.
Speaking at a news conference on Saturday, White did not say whether he would accept. He said he already had a lot of commitments and expected to discuss the matter at a meeting with Trump on Monday.

Trump later said White was coming to Washington on Monday for other reasons and that he would meet him there. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also reported Trump’s “kidding” remarks under similar headlines.
The press secretary post has been vacant since October, when Katie Zacharia left after less than five days. She had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who held the job from the start of Trump’s second term.

The episode follows Republican losses in the midterm elections, which cost the party its majority in both houses of Congress. White runs the UFC and PowerSlap, has recently launched the boxing promotion Zuffa Boxing, and sits on the board of Meta. He spoke at Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
items.cav: The detailed account comes from the BBC; the Guardian and Al Jazeera are represented only by short summaries, so their wording is not verified beyond the headlines. Whether White will take any role remains unresolved, and Trump’s Saturday post sits uneasily with his Sunday description of the offer as a joke.
items.op: A press secretary speaks for the government to the public every day, so the appointment deserves a transparent process rather than a social media post later described as a joke. When a public offer is made and then waved off, citizens cannot tell what is real. Voters are owed statements they can take at face value.

items.t: Kraków market square shooting suspect dies in hospital, Polish police say
items.s: A 24-year-old Polish man suspected of killing six people in a shooting in central Kraków has died in hospital, police said on Monday. Investigators are still working to establish his motive.
p: The suspect was wounded in an exchange of fire with police on Saturday and died early on Monday, according to the Lesser Poland police, who announced the death on X. Authorities have not yet officially named him. Doctors had earlier described his condition as critical.

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time in Kraków’s Main Market Square, a busy area of the Old Town that is usually crowded with tourists. Police said the gunman drove at high speed into the square and fired at random, and that he kept shooting even after being wounded by officers. Armed officers engaged him and he was shot within minutes, officials said.

Police said three bodies were found at the suspect’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town north of Kraków. On Sunday they confirmed the dead were his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his sister, 21. Police said the injuries appeared to be gunshot wounds, and the cause and nature of the deaths are still being clarified.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the gunman was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held radical, ultranationalist views. Prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said it would continue despite the suspect’s death and would aim to establish whether he acted alone. He asked for “restraint” and said evidence would not be disclosed for now.

Six people were killed, four of them Polish, along with an Austrian woman aged 51 and a British man aged 32. Reports differ on the number injured, with most citing 15 or 16. Two police officers were among the wounded, and both were reported to have come out of medically induced comas on Sunday. Two surgeons who were eating nearby treated victims on the street.

The suspect reportedly held a firearms permit. Four firearms, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, were found in his car, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, according to the spokesperson for the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Poland declared two days of national mourning, and flags were lowered to half mast. Mourners left candles in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the attack as terrorism, the deadliest in Poland since the end of communism in 1989, according to Euronews.
items.cav: Sources disagree on the number of injured (15 or 16), on the distance from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski to Kraków (about 100 miles or 150 kilometres), and on the gender split of the Polish victims. The motive remains unconfirmed; the early ministerial description has not been backed by released evidence, and details about the permit and the surgeons come from media reports.
items.op: A suspect’s death ends one threat but not the questions. Officials offered early labels for motive before prosecutors said the evidence was still under review. Public trust depends on the terrorism inquiry establishing, in open and checkable terms, who acted, why, and whether anyone else was involved. Those answers, not the speed of the labelling, will decide how this case is remembered.

items.t: Seven dead and more than 100 injured as two trains collide south of Cairo
items.s: Seven people were killed and at least 125 were injured when two passenger trains collided on Sunday in Giza province, Egypt. Rail workers began repairing the damaged track the following day.
p: The crash took place on Sunday near Al-Ayyat, roughly 52 kilometres south of the Egyptian capital, according to Euronews. The Transport Ministry said a northbound-to-Fayoum service ran into the back of a passenger train that was standing still and headed for Aswan. The BBC placed the scene between the Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations and reported that several carriages came off the rails and tumbled down an embankment.

Photographs from the site showed people looking through overturned carriages for anyone still hurt, as a large emergency operation got going. Egypt’s health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, told the BBC that patients were being treated for fractures and head trauma, and that local hospitals had been told to stay prepared for a surge in arrivals. Egypt’s Health Ministry later said more than 70 hurt passengers had left hospital after care.

The BBC reported that the driver of one of the trains was among the dead, a claim it attributed to the ministry. Euronews did not mention this. The Egyptian Red Crescent said its teams were offering relief and emotional help to the injured and their relatives at the scene.

Ahmad Othman Abu Emran, an eyewitness, told Euronews he was working in a field close by when the collision happened. He recalled the force of the impact and the noise of carriages flipping, then ran over to assist, calling what he saw devastating.

President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has called for an urgent inquiry into what caused the collision. The BBC quoted him as saying that anyone found to have been careless should be held to account. The same outlet reported demands in Egypt that the transport minister step down, though neither report says whether the government has answered those demands.

Euronews said crews, cranes and rail workers were clearing the wreckage and fixing the track on Monday. The BBC noted that services between Giza and Upper Egypt had been halted, and the railway authority had not said how long the stoppage would last. Euronews added that the crash has revived concern about upkeep and management across the country’s rail system, and it recalled a 2002 fire that killed more than 300 people. The BBC put the official toll from that disaster above 370.
items.cav: The sources differ on several points: the injury count (125 versus more than 100), the direction of the trains, and the death toll in the 2002 fire. The claim that the train driver died comes only from the BBC, and the reports on resignation calls are not followed by any official response.
items.op: Egypt’s rail network has faced safety criticism for years, and the families of the dead deserve a clear account of what went wrong. Sisi’s order for an urgent investigation is a start, but accountability depends on publishing the findings and naming any failures. Otherwise the next collision will bring the same grief and the same promises.

items.t: Nvidia opens independent probe into CEO Jensen Huang over affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang, who has admitted an affair with a woman that US officials reportedly believe was spying for China. The case raises questions for the world's most valuable chipmaker and the wider race for advanced chips.
p: Nvidia’s board said the inquiry was opened in light of recent reporting that Huang had been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” It said it had “no reason to believe” that national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised, but that the review would examine all available information. The investigation is being led by independent board members and an external law firm.

In a letter to employees, Huang said he took “full responsibility” for his actions. He said he had been unfaithful to his wife, apologised to his family, and acknowledged that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to employees, the board and shareholders. According to Euronews, the letter did not name the woman involved or her reported ties to Beijing.

The Financial Times first reported the affair. It identified the woman as Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm that has become Nvidia’s largest customer in Southeast Asia. Alice Huang is not related to the CEO, according to the BBC. The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believed she was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. These claims have not been confirmed publicly by US intelligence officials.

Beijing has rejected the allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the claims were entirely groundless and intended to smear China. Reports said US officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before President Donald Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Trump has defended Huang, describing him as a “fine person” and saying he had not spoken to him about the matter. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence sooner, Trump said he did not think so. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on the matter.

The affair comes as Nvidia, valued at about $5 trillion, faces doubts over the sustainability of a massive spending boom and a sell-off in related stocks. Huang has lobbied Trump to ease chip export restrictions on China, and the sales deal has been slowed by strict licence reviews. Analysts said Huang’s influence could be weakened, and that the company depends heavily on him, with no obvious successor.
items.cav: The espionage claims come from press reports citing US officials, and the officials have not commented publicly. Nvidia’s conclusion that secrets were not compromised is its own view and has not been tested by the investigation. Some details, including the memo and Trump’s briefing, rest on second-hand reporting.
items.op: A chipmaker’s chief executive is not above scrutiny when national security may be at stake. Nvidia’s investigation is a start, but its findings should be made public as far as possible. Shareholders and the public deserve to know whether a foreign power gained access to sensitive technology, not only whether the company is comfortable with its own answer.

items.t: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang faces questions over alleged Chinese espionage link
items.s: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether chief executive Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The allegations centre on a Chinese businesswoman, and the company’s shares fell more than 4 percent in overnight trading.
p: Scrutiny has landed on Nvidia’s chief executive after reports that a Chinese woman he had a romantic involvement with may have been collecting information for Beijing. Huang, who helped found the chipmaker more than thirty years ago, has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. The firm, however, says it sees no grounds to think sensitive US material or proprietary data has been exposed.

The board has commissioned a review, led by a committee of directors with outside lawyers, to establish whether Huang was the subject of a foreign spying effort. The inquiry followed media coverage tying him to Alice Huang, who previously worked as an executive at a data centre firm based in Singapore. Reports indicate the two are not related, despite sharing a surname. Huang has pledged to cooperate and to keep leading the company.

The claims originated with a New York Times investigation published last month. That outlet cited American intelligence officials who believed Beijing had enlisted Alice Huang to learn about the chief executive and perhaps sway Nvidia’s chip sales into China. Exactly what she obtained, whether anything sensitive reached Chinese hands, and how much Huang understood about any scheme are still unknown.

Huang told Bloomberg News in late October that his dealings with her were tied to Megaspeed, her company, and were ordinary. According to the Times, Megaspeed became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying roughly $4.8bn of equipment. American authorities have reportedly examined Megaspeed since 2024, suspecting it helped China acquire top Nvidia processors despite export controls. No criminal charges against either Huang have been reported.

Alice Huang, also called Huang Le, has not commented on the espionage allegations, and her whereabouts are unknown. An entry in a Chinese investment database lists earlier roles at HSBC and Chinese broadcasters, though AFP said it could not verify those details independently.

Politicians from both major parties are weighing in. Republican members of Congress have asked Huang to appear before lawmakers on 18 November, arguing that China’s possible access to sensitive American technology is at stake. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers from the company and urged passage of tougher rules to keep advanced US technology away from China.

Investors reacted quickly, with Nvidia’s market value of $4.5 trillion sliding more than 4 percent in overnight trading into Monday. Chris Beauchamp of IG Group said it was too early to tell whether the episode would prove a “major turning point” for the company.
items.cav: The sources do not establish what information, if any, was passed to Beijing, nor what Huang knew. Much of the espionage account rests on anonymous US intelligence officials as reported by the New York Times, and details of Alice Huang’s background are unverified. Her side of the story has not been heard.
items.op: Allegations of foreign espionage touching a company central to US chip policy are a matter of public interest, not private scandal. The independent review and congressional testimony should be conducted in the open, with findings published. Investors, lawmakers and the public deserve clear answers rather than assurances from the company.

items.t: Four killed in Gaza as sand embankment collapses onto displaced families’ tents after heavy rain
items.s: Four people, including three children, died when a sand embankment fell onto tents at a displaced families’ camp in central Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. The collapse came after heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across the territory.
p: The health ministry says a woman and three children were killed on Sunday night when earth piled up in a sand embankment gave way onto tents at a camp south of Deir al-Balah. Five people were reportedly pulled out alive after the collapse.

The disaster followed torrential rain the previous day, which reportedly swamped tens of thousands of tents throughout Gaza and left many displaced Palestinians with nowhere dry to sleep. According to the Civil Defence service, water reached depths of up to 1.5 metres in places, and its responders could attend to just 10% of the 2,100 emergency calls they received.

Footage circulated online showed people searching for survivors by the light of mobile phones, picking through boulders, sand and crushed tents. Mustafa al-Masri, a rescuer, told the BBC that the rescue crews and young men from the camp had to reach the trapped people by hand, because the mound was so large and spread so wide that nobody knew how to start.

The official count has changed. The Civil Defence first said that two women and three children had died, but on Monday morning the health ministry said only one woman was among the dead. The names it has given are Tahrir Nabhan, Mariam Nabhan, her brother Salah and Habiba al-Zein.

The Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, urged international bodies to supply secure shelters and relocate tents away from sandy ground, slopes and any spot prone to collapse. Karl Baker of the International Organization for Migration described the aid now entering Gaza as far too limited, comparing it to the most minimal of plasters and calling for more donations in kind and funding.

Cogat, the Israeli military unit that coordinates aid deliveries, said more than 91,000 tents and other supplies had reached Gaza under its winter preparation scheme. It also said Israel would bar any equipment that Hamas or other armed factions could use for military ends. The UN estimates that roughly 80% of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed or damaged, and that 1.2 million of the more than 1.9 million displaced people live in tents or improvised shelters.

Masri said he had been forced out of Beit Hanoun in the north but remained in central Gaza, having found no other place he considered suitable. The UN warns that conditions stay grave despite the October 2025 ceasefire, as Israeli strikes keep hitting populated areas.
items.cav: The casualty figures differ between sources: the Civil Defence first reported five deaths, while the health ministry later reported four, and the sources do not explain the revision in detail. Both the health ministry and the Civil Defence operate under Hamas-run authorities, and the Cogat figures on deliveries are the Israeli military’s own claims that the sources do not independently verify.
items.op: Shelter for displaced families should not depend on whether a camp happens to sit below an unstable mound. The shift from five reported deaths to four shows why early figures from every side need checking against clear records. Disputes over what aid may enter should be settled openly, with published rules, not left to be argued through statements after each tragedy.

items.t: Krakow shooting: surgeons who were lunching nearby describe treating gunman and officers
items.s: Two surgeons who were eating near Krakow’s Main Market Square when a gunman opened fire say they treated the attacker and two police officers at the scene. One colleague says his actions undoubtedly saved an officer’s life.
p: Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families on Saturday when they heard gunshots, according to local media reports cited by the BBC. The shooting killed six people and injured 15, the BBC reported.

Pędziwiatr told the Polish outlet Fakt that his son ran up to him and said people were being shot and falling to the ground. When the two doctors reached the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers who had been shot while subduing him.

Wierdak worked on an officer who had been shot in the chest. Describing the emergency treatment, he told Fakt that he “stuffed all the bandages” into the wound. He said that without this, “I don’t know how things would have turned out”, because an ambulance had a long wait to arrive.

Pędziwiatr said he telephoned John Paul II Hospital, where the thoracic and cardiac surgery department is based, and insisted the officer be taken there. In his view, it offered the best chance of survival because specialists there treated that type of injury.

The two officers have been named as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański. On Sunday they came out of comas. Prime Minister Donald Tusk had earlier hailed both as heroes for preventing further deaths. (The BBC report describes the prime minister’s praise as “true heroes”; the officers’ recovery is reported by the BBC but details of their condition beyond this are not given in the evidence.)

Prosecutors said the 25-year-old Polish attacker remains in critical condition. They had earlier said he was inspired by “far-right ideologies” and have opened a terror investigation. The National Public Prosecutor’s Office is leading the inquiry through a unit that handles terrorist offences. The attacker is a suspect and has not been tried.

Among the dead were a British national and an Austrian woman, along with four Poles. Six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers, who were on a city break nearby, also gave medical help after the shooting, RTÉ News reported, quoting officer James McConnell. They provided CPR and haemorrhage control.

Witnesses described panic in the square. London resident Ruby Catherine Warren said she heard gunfire and ran with her friends until they reached a hotel to hide. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, said he was inside a nearby McDonald’s when he heard multiple gunshots, and later saw a body covered in foil blankets about 20 metres away.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the attacker acted alone, and the “far-right” motive is a prosecutors’ statement made before any trial. Several details, including the surgeons’ accounts, come through local media reports and may not be fully verified.
items.op: Heroism at the scene deserves praise, but it should not end the story. Prosecutors must explain the motive and the attacker’s path clearly, and the public deserves a transparent account of how the response unfolded.

items.t: Eisenkot Begins Bid to Form Israeli Government Without a Clear Majority
items.s: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has been given the mandate to form Israel’s next government, despite his bloc lacking a clear majority in parliament. He says Benjamin Netanyahu has brought the country to a historic crisis.
p: Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to allies of Benjamin Netanyahu. He said the veteran prime minister had led the country into a historic crisis.

Eisenkot, 66, leads the Yashar party and has promised to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation. President Isaac Herzog formally gave him a mandate and 28 days to build a government, even though his bloc does not have a clear majority. Herzog can grant a 14-day extension before the mandate must pass to someone else.

Speaking at a ceremony at the presidential office, Eisenkot said the country was “approaching a point of no return.” He called for a “national emergency government” and said it would require “creative and unconventional political steps.”

According to the Guardian, Eisenkot has three possible routes. He could agree a power-sharing deal with Netanyahu, win support from Arab-led parties, which several members of his own bloc oppose, or reach an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, who want military exemptions for their community.

The October election left neither side with a majority. Eisenkot’s opposition bloc won 48 of the 120 seats, while Netanyahu’s camp took 53. Both Arab-majority lists endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog, and they could now act as kingmakers. Eisenkot has set conditions for any Arab party joining his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and labelling Hamas a terrorist organisation. The more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party has already said it will not sit with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot has also appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud and to the far-right party of finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, but only on the condition that he serve as prime minister. Netanyahu called for a national unity government with Eisenkot on Saturday, though it is unclear whether the two can agree on power sharing. Netanyahu is expected to keep up pressure, warning that any alliance with Arab parties would be a betrayal.

Netanyahu has repeatedly said the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, but the Guardian reports he has offered little to no evidence. Israel’s Shin Bet security agency is investigating possible foreign interference. The Central Elections Committee and Herzog say the vote was valid, and that any wrongdoing found would not have changed the result significantly.

Eisenkot, who was military chief from 2015 to 2019, has vowed to crack down on extremist settlers in the West Bank and has described recent attacks as Jewish terror. He opposes a Palestinian state and wants to end Hamas rule in Gaza. If he cannot assemble a coalition, Israel faces fresh elections, having already held five between 2019 and 2022.
items.cav: The Guardian is the detailed source here; the second outlet’s brief summary adds only that Eisenkot has up to six weeks, which matches the 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu’s claim of a stolen election is his own and is not supported by the evidence; the outcome of the Shin Bet investigation is not reported.
items.op: Israel’s coalition arithmetic should not override the basic question of how the vote was run and who is accountable for it. Netanyahu’s unsupported fraud claims make transparent answers from the Shin Bet and the elections committee more urgent. Any coalition, whoever leads it, must be judged by whether it restores public trust.

items.t: Collision of two trains south of Cairo kills at least seven, officials say
items.s: Officials say at least seven people died and over a hundred were hurt when two trains struck each other on Sunday south of Cairo. Egypt’s president has called for a swift inquiry.
p: The collision took place in al-Ayyat, a district of Giza province roughly 30 miles south of Cairo. Citing the transport ministry, reports say a service bound for Fayoum, in the south-west, slammed into the back of a train that was headed for Aswan, in the south.

Officials said an inspection showed the Cairo-Aswan train was standing still on that same line when the impact occurred. The reporting does not explain why it was stopped there, or how the other train ended up on that track.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat, told the Guardian that bystanders hurried over, dragged survivors out and summoned ambulances. He claimed to have watched around 80 casualties being driven to hospital, and said some travellers were caught in a carriage of the motionless train and did not survive.

In a post on social media, President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi said he had instructed investigators to act quickly. The Egyptian railway authority said rescue crews and cranes were deployed to remove the debris and bring services back to timetable as soon as possible.

Rail accidents are a recurring problem in Egypt, where the network has been criticised for poor management and inadequate equipment upkeep. Authorities have launched modernisation programmes in recent years. In September, two freight trains crashed in the same district, leaving the driver and his assistant injured.
The country’s worst rail tragedy remains the 2002 blaze on an overnight train from Cairo to southern Egypt, which claimed more than 300 lives.
items.cav: The death toll of at least seven and the figure of more than 100 injured come from officials; the claim of 80 hospital transfers comes from one resident’s account. The cause of the collision has not been established, and the reporting does not say whether the findings will be made public.
items.op: Seven deaths and more than 100 injuries require more than a routine promise of inquiry. The investigation the president ordered should publish its findings, explain why a stationary train was struck on the same track, and name any maintenance failures. Repeated crashes make openness the only credible answer.

items.t: More than 200 tarantula sightings reported in Austria since September
items.s: Austrian citizens have reported more than 200 tarantula sightings since early September, and experts have verified 175 of them. Most reports come from Styria, Lower Austria and Burgenland.
p: Austria has logged more than 200 tarantula sightings over roughly two months, according to reports gathered through naturbeobachtung.at, a citizen science platform. Experts have verified 175 of them.
By region, Styria in the southeast leads with 66 reports. Lower Austria counted 49 and Burgenland 43, while Carinthia also registered sightings.

Autumn is the busiest season for the spiders, which look for protected spots to pass the winter. Occasionally they end up inside homes, apartments and garages. In nature they normally retreat to burrows dug underground and to cracks in rocks.

Among the standout finds was a South Russian tarantula in Tulln, Lower Austria, well to the northwest of its usual range. Carolina Trcka-Rojas of the Austrian Nature Conservation Association said no sightings had previously been recorded in that surrounding area. In late August, a black-bellied tarantula turned up in Stossau, in the lower Gail valley, the species' westernmost known Austrian record.

Two tarantula species are generally found in Austria. Both belong to the wolf spider group and may bite when provoked, an event described as uncommon. A bite can hurt and leave redness and swelling, but it is generally not dangerous for healthy adults.

Historical records place the first documented South Russian tarantula in Austria in the early 1920s, near Lake Neusiedl and Vienna. The black-bellied species was first recorded in Styria during the 1970s.
Austria is not alone in this trend. A 2025 study reported that tarantulas in Czechia are spreading again after decades of decline, and researchers point to warmer, drier summers as a major factor.
items.cav: The figures come from a citizen science platform, so they reflect reported sightings rather than measured population changes, and the sources do not say whether the tarantula population is actually growing. The Austrian counts are not broken down by species.
items.op: Open citizen data helps scientists track wildlife, but it should be read with care. Authorities and researchers should publish clear methods and verified counts, so that public alarm does not outrun the evidence.

items.t: Diwali lights up India as air pollution clouds the festival in Delhi and Mumbai
items.s: Millions across India are marking Diwali with lamps, fireworks and sweets, but the celebrations are taking place amid rising concern about air quality, especially in the north. The Supreme Court has allowed certified “green” firecrackers in Delhi for a limited period.
p: Across India, millions of people are taking part in Diwali, a Hindu festival held on a moonless night in the month of Kartik. Homes, shrines, workplaces and public streets glow with lamps and bright lights, a display meant to represent the defeat of darkness by illumination.

Customs vary from region to region and from community to community, yet most celebrations include prayer, get-togethers at home, sweets shared among relatives and friends, and firecrackers. In the days beforehand, people tidy and adorn their houses with flowers and clay lamps called diyas, colourful floor designs appear at doorways, and shops fill with buyers.

According to the BBC, the festivities are overshadowed by worsening air quality, particularly in northern India. Weather patterns and the burning of crop stubble are cited as contributing factors, and fireworks set off during the holiday can add to the problem. Delhi's pollution has reached hazardous levels, which the broadcaster describes as the worst Diwali for air in a decade, and recent measures do not appear to have worked. Mumbai, the financial capital, has also recorded high readings in recent weeks.

India's Supreme Court, ruling on Monday, granted a temporary exemption allowing certified “green” firecrackers to be made, sold and set off in Delhi and nearby areas. These devices are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. Critics doubt how much they help, and they worry that ordinary firecrackers could still reach the capital from neighbouring states.

Beyond the fireworks, the festival commemorates Lord Ram's return to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the chief villain of the Ramayana epic. The celebrations unfold over several days. Dhanteras, which began on 6 November, is a day for buying gold, silver or new utensils, considered lucky. Chhoti Diwali brings lamps and, in some homes, firecrackers. The main day involves evening prayers to Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, followed by festive meals. The final day, Bhai Dooj, honours the bond between brothers and sisters.

Sikhs and Jains also mark the period. Sikhs commemorate the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th century. For Jains, the day is linked to Lord Mahavira's attainment of moksha, or liberation from rebirth. Indian communities abroad hold their own gatherings and exchange gifts.

The occasion is also seen as a favourable time for new purchases. India's stock exchanges will hold a one-hour special trading session, known as Muhurat trading, on 8 November this year. In Nepal, where the festival is called Tihar, pets and street animals are honoured.
items.cav: The source does not say how the “most polluted in a decade” judgement was measured or by whom, and it gives no current air quality readings. The 20-30% emissions figure for green firecrackers comes without independent testing details, and the critics' objections are reported without specifics.
items.op: Celebration should not come at the cost of breathable air for millions of residents. If pollution rules are to mean anything, the court's temporary permission must be paired with transparent monitoring and enforcement, so that citizens can see whether the measures are working.

items.t: Herzog taps Gadi Eisenkot to try forming Israel’s next government
items.s: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has asked Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to attempt to build a government after an October election left neither him nor Benjamin Netanyahu with a clear route to power. If Eisenkot succeeds, he would replace Netanyahu as prime minister.
p: Isaac Herzog has selected Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and the most prominent challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu, to attempt to assemble a cabinet. According to the president’s office, Herzog told Eisenkot of his decision late on Saturday. The formal handover was scheduled for a ceremony on Sunday at the presidential residence in Jerusalem.

The Knesset has been stalemated since the vote on 27 October, when Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist alliance lost its parliamentary majority. Even so, his camp won 53 of the 120 seats, the largest share in the chamber. Eisenkot’s opposition grouping took 48, so neither side reaches the 61 seats needed to govern.

Eisenkot, 66 and a former army chief, wrote on X that the moment called for a government of national urgency. He also received the backing of both Arab-majority lists, which posted record results and could now decide who governs. Analysts in the sources describe three possible paths: a power-sharing arrangement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties, or a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties that want military exemptions for their community.

The route ahead is difficult. Eisenkot has attached conditions to any Arab party joining his coalition, among them acknowledging Israel as a Jewish state and classifying Hamas as a terrorist group. Yisrael Beiteinu, one of his partners, has ruled out sitting in a government with Arab-led parties. Equal military service, including an end to the ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions, was a core theme of his campaign.

Netanyahu has repeatedly said Arab parties stole the election, yet the report says he has produced little to no proof. Israel’s Shin Bet security service has opened an inquiry into possible foreign meddling. The Central Elections Committee and Herzog maintain the vote was valid and that any irregularities would not have materially altered the outcome. Netanyahu has called for a unity government with Eisenkot, but it is unclear whether the two can agree terms on sharing power.

Eisenkot has promised to curb violent extremist settlers in the West Bank, whose attacks on Palestinians he has described as Jewish terror. He opposes a Palestinian state and has pledged to end Hamas’s control of Gaza. He has 28 days to gather a majority, and Herzog can extend that by 14 days. If no candidate succeeds, Israel faces another election.
items.cav: The sources do not establish whether Eisenkot can assemble a majority, and Netanyahu’s fraud claims remain unsupported by the evidence. The Shin Bet inquiry is ongoing, so its findings are unknown. The count of this as a sixth election since 2019 is an inference from the five elections the report mentions between 2019 and 2022.
items.op: Whoever governs Israel next will be judged on whether they respect the process that produced them. Unsubstantiated claims that an election was stolen erode public trust, and so do backroom deals dressed up as national unity. Israelis deserve a coalition built on open terms that can withstand scrutiny.

items.t: Cop31 talks in Turkey open with pressure for visible climate progress
items.s: Negotiators from roughly 190 countries convene in Antalya on Monday for Cop31, and the host says the summit has to deliver results people can verify. The meeting opens while the strongest El Niño on record is still strengthening.
p: The UN climate conference gets under way on Monday in Antalya, Turkey, drawing world leaders and delegations from about 190 countries. The host has argued that the gathering must yield something measurable that ordinary people can recognise as genuine progress.

The arrangement is unusual. Turkey is the venue, but Australia will preside over the formal negotiations, a split agreed last year after the two countries put forward competing bids. Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and the president of negotiations, told the Guardian that the talks need concrete steps on cutting emissions and on finance, and that they must move beyond the previous Cops.

Canberra intends to push for a robust result that addresses low-lying Pacific nations, which it describes as facing an existential danger. Bowen said that only 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance reaches small island developing states for adaptation. Climate advocates, along with more than 500 Australian scientists, counter that the country cannot credibly press this case while it keeps approving new coal and gas developments.

Adão Soares Barbosa, who chairs the Least Developed Countries group of 44 nations, framed the stakes in starker terms. He said that limiting warming to 1.5C, providing finance that poor countries can count on, strengthening adaptation and tackling loss and damage are essential for survival.

The United States will again stay away, the second year in a row. A White House spokesperson said the administration wants nothing to do with what it called “extremist climate policies”. Twenty Democratic members of Congress will attend instead. The Guardian reports that their party’s strong showing in the recent midterm elections could allow them to block attempts to roll back pollution rules and to cut support for clean energy.

The summit’s backdrop is grim. According to the article, more than 50,000 people died in Europe this summer from heatwaves, and a glacier collapse in Nepal set off a landslide that killed more than 1,500 people. The El Niño, which has yet to peak, is described by the article as set to claim hundreds of thousands of lives, though it does not explain how that estimate was reached.

Turkey, the second host, is pushing for wider adoption of electric vehicles and heat pumps. A proposed goal of supplying 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035 is expected to be discussed, although some countries oppose it. Both presidencies depend heavily on fossil fuels, and the article says Australia’s centre-left government is off course for its 2050 net zero target.
items.cav: The article relies on statements from the host, campaigners and officials, and it does not independently verify the death tolls or the El Niño projection. It does not say who produced the 50,000 and 1,500 figures, so they should be read as reported rather than confirmed.
items.op: A summit is only as credible as the promises it keeps. Cop31 should be judged on cuts and finance that reach vulnerable countries, not on speeches from hosts whose fossil fuel industries sit at odds with their message. Clear public accounting of who pays and who receives is the measure that counts.

items.t: European and world leaders offer condolences after Krakow shooting
items.s: Leaders from across Europe and beyond have expressed condolences and solidarity with Poland after a shooting in Krakow that killed people and injured others. Their statements focused on grief and support rather than on details of the attack.
p: News of the shooting in Krakow spread quickly, and governments across Europe responded within a short time. According to the reports, representatives of several European countries, along with the European Union and the United States, expressed sympathy for those affected and condemned violence in all its forms.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was moved by the events and described Germany as a friend and partner of Poland. French President Emmanuel Macron wrote of his shock and emotion and pledged solidarity with the Polish people and the families of the victims.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the attack a cowardly and unacceptable act of violence. She said her government would defend its security and freedom against every form of terror. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was shocked and saddened, and that the United Kingdom stands with the Polish people.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda, Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban also sent messages of condolence and solidarity. Lithuania’s statement expressed support for President Karol Nawrocki and the Polish people.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen thanked the police officers who, she said, acted at the risk of their lives. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola also thanked the police and emergency services for their rapid intervention and for bringing the situation under control. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the tragedy would be felt far beyond Poland’s borders.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as a shocking crime and said there was no justification for it. He added that he trusted the perpetrator would face justice. US Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said America stands by Poland in this dark hour.

The statements do not give a full account of what happened in Krakow, including the number of dead and injured, the location of the shooting beyond the Main Market Square, or whether a suspect has been arrested or charged. Several leaders referred to the victims without describing the circumstances of their deaths.
items.cav: The sources are mostly leaders’ statements and do not describe the attack in detail, such as casualty figures, a motive or the status of any suspect. Zelenskyy’s reference to a perpetrator is a statement of expectation, not a confirmed identification. Details should be checked against official Polish reports.
items.op: Solidarity after a shooting is easy to declare and harder to sustain. What matters now is that Polish authorities explain who was responsible, how the attack unfolded and whether any security failures need answering. Leaders who promise justice should be judged by whether the investigation is open to scrutiny.

items.t: Trump publicly offers UFC boss Dana White the White House press secretary job
items.s: President Donald Trump has publicly offered the White House press secretary role to Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. White has neither accepted nor publicly rejected the offer, and says he will meet Trump in Washington on Monday.
p: Trump announced the offer in a Truth Social post on Saturday, calling White “a violent Fighter and Warrior” and saying he would be a press secretary unlike any other. In the same post he wrote, “Dana, please take the job!”

Speaking to reporters in London after a boxing event, White did not go into detail. He said he was flying to Washington and would meet Trump on Monday, adding that the two would likely have more to discuss afterwards. Earlier he had shared an image of himself at the White House briefing room lectern on Instagram, captioned “On to the next chapter.” The BBC noted it was unclear whether that post was tongue-in-cheek.

Trump also asked White to bring six UFC fighters to work as aides, writing, “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left.” According to the Guardian, two of the fighters named, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov, are not American, a point Trump acknowledged in his post.

The announcement came days after Trump’s Republicans lost their congressional majorities in the midterm elections. The Guardian reported that some observers questioned whether the offer was a serious plan or an attempt to change the subject.

The press secretary post has been vacant since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia left after less than five days in the job, following a shaky first briefing. Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, stepped down in August to focus on her family, according to the reports.

CNN, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that White had turned down the offer, and the Guardian said one aide to the president had described it as a joke. Neither claim has been confirmed by White, and the sources do not agree on whether White has formally answered. The Guardian also noted that the government post pays $195,000 a year, while White’s UFC role has reportedly earned him a fortune estimated at more than $600m.

White and Trump have been close for years. White has spoken at Trump’s Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and the UFC has hosted events at the White House in June, according to DW and the Guardian.
items.cav: The report that White turned down the job comes from CNN via unnamed sources and is not confirmed by White, and it is unclear whether Trump’s offer was serious. The $600m fortune figure is an estimate reported by the Guardian and is not verified.
items.op: Presidents may choose their own aides, but the press secretary answers to reporters and the public, not to a friend’s showmanship. A job offered through a social media post is a poor substitute for open selection. Until any appointment is formal and explained, the public should treat this as a spectacle.

items.t: Eisenkot gets chance to form Israel’s next government as divided opposition weighs its options
items.s: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been asked to form a government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority. His path to power depends on parties whose positions sharply conflict.
p: After an inconclusive election in October, President Isaac Herzog chose the former military chief to try to build a government. The choice came on Saturday, after he had held consultations with the political parties. Eisenkot, who leads the Yashar party, now has 28 days to assemble a coalition, and he may ask for a further 14 days if he does not succeed in that time.

Writing on X, Eisenkot called for a national emergency government and said he would work hard to meet that goal. The 66-year-old faces a hard task, because many opposition parties disagree deeply on national security, religion and the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu commands the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist bloc has dropped from 64 seats in 2022 to 53, eight short of a majority. His Likud is still the largest single party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21.

Arab-led parties may now decide who governs. Ra’am and the Joint List, which together hold 19 seats, have backed Eisenkot’s attempt, which would lift the anti-Netanyahu camp to 67 seats. Eisenkot has ruled out including Arab parties in his cabinet, however, and Avigdor Lieberman has repeatedly opposed a minority government that relies on them.

Eisenkot’s possible core partners are his own party, Yair Golan’s Democrats, Naftali Bennett’s Together party and Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu. Golan’s Democrats have been more open to working with Ra’am and the Joint List, and Golan has argued that Netanyahu’s split between Jewish and Arab voters should be rejected.

If a full coalition cannot be formed, Eisenkot could lead a minority government that Arab-led parties support from outside, without necessarily taking cabinet seats. A second option would bring in the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which hold 13 seats between them. That would give his bloc exactly 61, but it would require concessions on military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox students, a question that has long split Israeli politics.

The reporting also recalls that Ra’am joined a Bennett-led government in 2021 as the first independent Arab party to do so. That administration collapsed after about 18 months, largely over settlements in the occupied West Bank and the question of Palestinian statehood.
items.cav: The seat counts and party positions are those reported after consultations and could change during negotiations. Lieberman’s openness to compromise on conscription is described only as an indication, and it is unclear whether Arab-led support would be formal or informal.
items.op: Israeli voters have signalled a wish for change, but a government built on vetoes and on silence about the Arab parties’ role would be fragile. Its terms should be published and debated openly in the Knesset, because transparent bargaining serves democracy better than backroom deals.

items.t: Krakow square shooting leaves six dead; suspect’s family found dead at home
items.s: A gunman drove into Krakow’s Main Market Square and opened fire, killing six people and injuring many more, according to Polish officials. Three further bodies were later found at the suspect’s home.
p: The shooting took place on Saturday afternoon, shortly before 3 p.m. local time, in Krakow’s Main Market Square, a busy central point popular with tourists. According to police, a man drove into the square and began firing at people from his car. Video footage shows people running as gunfire sounds, and a passing tram was struck, shattering its windows, though no passengers were reported injured.

Armed officers responded and exchanged fire with the suspect, who was wounded and arrested. Officials said his shooting stopped what could have been a larger massacre. Six people, including a British national, are confirmed dead. Sixteen people were taken to hospital, among them two police officers, the suspect, and several foreign nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, according to the interior ministry. Officials said the officers’ condition was serious, with one described as critical.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attack an act of terrorism, and prosecutors in Krakow have opened an investigation into whether it qualifies as a terrorist offence. Police said the suspect’s car was checked for explosive devices and none were found. Nearby residents were evacuated during the operation, and the square was closed.

Police later found three bodies at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 200 km from Krakow. Officials said they were his parents and sister. Reports differ on the sister’s age, with one source saying 21 and another 20. Police said the suspect held a firearms licence and may have used a weapon covered by it. Polish media has reported he may have obtained the weapons from the family home. Those claims have not been confirmed by officials.

The interior minister said the suspect appeared to hold very radical views and was drawn to far-right ideologies, and a minister described him as an ultra-nationalist, without giving details. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz denied reports that the suspect was a soldier. Police have not officially confirmed the suspect’s name, and his age is reported as 24 by one outlet and 25 by another.
Poland has declared two days of national mourning, with flags at half-mast and entertainment events cancelled.
items.cav: Several details remain unconfirmed or conflicting, including the suspect’s age, his sister’s age, the number and nationalities of the injured, and the officers’ condition. The claims about his motive and his family home come from ministers and unnamed or secondary reporting, and the investigation has not established a full account.
items.op: Krakow’s residents and visitors deserve clear, timely answers about how a licensed gunman reached the square with military-style weapons. Officials should publish what they know about the permit and the family’s access to the arsenal. Transparency now is the surest way to rebuild public trust.

items.t: Poland mourns after Krakow Main Square shooting that killed six; terror probe opened
items.s: Poland has entered national mourning after a gunman killed six people and wounded 15 in Krakow’s Main Square. Prosecutors have opened a terror investigation.
p: Saturday’s gunfire in Krakow’s Old Town left six people dead and 15 injured, and the country responded with a two-day period of mourning that began on Sunday. The attack took place at Rynek Glowny, the central plaza of Poland’s second-largest city, a site that draws large numbers of visitors. On Sunday, people paying respects had laid candles there, and banners in black appeared across the city beside national flags with dark ribbons.

Investigators describe the gunman as a 24-year-old man who wore military-style clothing during the assault. He allegedly fired on passers-by at random while driving around the plaza. Two officers who moved to confront him were hurt and are being treated in hospital, and one of them is in a critical state, prompting an appeal for blood donors.

Later, police reported finding three bodies at the suspect’s residence in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, roughly 150 kilometres north-east of Krakow. They identified them as his father, mother and sister. The sources do not explain how those deaths relate to the attack in the square.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has characterised the shooting as far-right terrorism. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski told a news conference that the suspect appeared to have been drawn to far-right ideology. Officials say he held right-wing extremist and ultranationalist beliefs, but authorities have not yet put forward a motive.

A British citizen was among those killed. Those injured included people from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, authorities said. A Krakow association representing horse-carriage drivers told the PAP news agency that several of its drivers were badly hurt.
Polish media have reported that the suspect had no criminal history. Parts of the square stayed cordoned off on Sunday morning while investigators continued their work.
items.cav: The suspect has not been charged in the sources, and his motive rests on officials’ statements rather than a published finding. The link between the deaths at the home and the square attack is not explained, and the clean criminal record comes from media reports rather than an official source.
items.op: Officials have already labelled this terrorism, so transparency matters now. The public deserves a clear account of the motive, the warning signs and how a man with no record reached this point. Anything less risks turning grief into rumour.

items.t: Herzog tasks Eisenkot with forming Israeli government after inconclusive vote
items.s: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has asked Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, to try to form a new government after an October election left neither main camp with a clear majority. Eisenkot now faces weeks of difficult talks.
p: Herzog's office said on Saturday evening that he had decided to give Eisenkot, a former military chief, the first chance to build a coalition. According to the statement, factions totalling 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset backed Eisenkot after consultations, while 46 supported Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Other outlets gave different totals for the two camps, and the figures should be read with that in mind.

Under Israeli rules, a candidate has 28 days to form a government, and the president can extend that by up to 14 days. If that fails, Herzog can offer the task to a second candidate, and the Knesset can later nominate a third. Reports put the overall timeline at roughly 100 days.

Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in the October 27 vote but remained the largest bloc. Likud won 27 seats, the single largest party. One report says Eisenkot's Yashar party took 21 seats, and his wider bloc won 48. Two Arab parties secured 19 seats between them, a result described as unprecedented.

Eisenkot has said he will do everything to form a government, but his options are narrow. He could try to govern with outside support from Arab parties, build a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties he has previously shunned, or join a unity government with Netanyahu, whom he has said he would not serve alongside. Analysts quoted in one report consider all three unlikely.

If he succeeds, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister from Israel’s Mizrahi community, Jews whose roots lie in the Middle East and North Africa. He is the son of Moroccan immigrants and is 66. His family has also paid a heavy price in the war in Gaza, with a son and two nephews killed there, according to one report.

Critics of Israel's conduct in Gaza say its campaign has caused destruction amounting to war crimes, a charge Israel disputes. The Gaza health ministry says more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed. Eisenkot has criticised settler violence in the West Bank, which he called “Jewish terror” encouraged by Netanyahu's government.
items.cav: The sources give different seat totals for the two blocs and for Yashar, and the 67-to-46 faction count in the Herzog statement does not match the 53-to-48 seat figures. The Gaza death toll is attributed to the Gaza health ministry and has not been independently verified in these reports.
items.op: Coalition arithmetic should be settled in public view, with clear accounting of who backs whom and on what terms. Voters deserve to know whether any future government rests on principle or on the bargaining power of its most extreme partners.

items.t: Trump’s weakened standing after the US midterms raises risks abroad, columnist argues
items.s: In a Guardian column, Simon Tisdall argues that the Democratic midterm successes have weakened Donald Trump at home and abroad, but that his lame duck status could still fuel new crises. The piece is opinion, and its forecasts are the columnist’s own.
p: Tisdall describes the midterm vote as a rebuke to Trump. In his account, the Democratic successes amounted to a personal repudiation of a president whose approval ratings he calls very low. He writes that people in many countries that suffered under Trump’s policies over the past two years welcomed the result as a shared moment of relief.

On Iran, Tisdall says many Iranians hoped Trump’s electoral setback might bring an end to what he calls a murderous war against Tehran’s regime. He warns that such hopes may be premature. In his view, Trump, who does not compromise easily when thwarted, could be pushed by Benjamin Netanyahu to defy chastened Republicans, including vice-president JD Vance, and resume or expand the conflict.

In Israel, Tisdall writes, many of the voters who backed change last week will welcome the weakening of Netanyahu’s most prominent backer in Washington. He argues that Netanyahu’s coalition remains in place and that any new Israeli government is likely to keep Palestinian rights in Gaza and the West Bank under denial, with broad US support.

On Russia and Ukraine, Tisdall reports that Ukrainians were optimistic that a Democratic-controlled Congress would curb what he describes as appeasement of Vladimir Putin. He argues that Putin, facing battlefield failures and economic problems, may want a deal while Trump is still in office, and that Trump’s negotiators could press Kyiv for territorial and other concessions.

Tisdall says that from January, when Democrats take charge of both chambers of Congress, Trump and senior officials are likely to face intense scrutiny over executive actions, budgets and alleged corruption and abuses of power. Some Democrats, he notes, want Trump impeached again. He suggests that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth could be an early casualty, though he expects Hegseth probably to avoid punishment.

Looking to 2028, Tisdall expects most US policies to change little. He lists possible shifts, including de-escalating tariff disputes with Europe and Canada, abandoning Nato commitments, or pursuing regime change in Cuba. He also argues that China’s Xi Jinping will continue to outmanoeuvre Trump, and that Democrats could move quickly to restore the overseas aid budget once they control spending.

Finally, Tisdall links the US result to other recent votes, citing progressive election victories in Hungary, Serbia and Brazil. He points to upcoming contests in Spain and, in 2027, France, as tests of whether far-right populist movements can be beaten again.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, not a news report, and its characterisations, such as ‘war of choice’ and ‘appeasement’, are the columnist’s own. The evidence gives no vote totals, seat numbers or formal White House response, and Trump’s denials are reported only as the columnist describes them. The impeachment demand is attributed only to ‘some Democrats’, and the forecasts about Russia, Iran and Israel are speculative.
items.op: The midterm result matters because it reminds leaders that power in a democracy is checked by voters and institutions, not by personal grievance. A Congress that now has a real chance to demand answers on war, Ukraine and spending should use that scrutiny openly and on the record. Washington must not let a lame duck president’s anger set the agenda abroad.

items.t: Houthi-linked media say 33 killed in Saudi air strikes near Sanaa; Riyadh has not commented
items.s: Houthi-aligned outlets report that at least 33 people, among them women and children, died in strikes on al-Shariyah, a town east of Sanaa. The Saudi-led coalition has not responded, and the toll has not been independently verified.
p: Houthi-aligned outlets say Saudi air strikes on al-Shariyah on Saturday killed at least 33 people, a group that included women and children. The town sits east of Yemen’s capital. Footage broadcast by Al Masirah, a station operated by the Houthis, showed rescuers lifting bodies, some of them small children, from the wreckage of several buildings, while wounded people were carried on stretchers into a hospital.

The Houthi health ministry put the number of wounded at 39. Its spokesman, Anees Alasbahi, told the Associated Press that Saudi Arabia was responsible for the strikes. The coalition, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has not issued a statement.

Every key claim in this account comes from the Houthi side: the death toll, the wounded count and the blame placed on Riyadh. The material available does not include an independent monitor’s assessment, and Saudi Arabia’s own account is absent.

The Houthis have governed Sanaa and large parts of western and northern Yemen since the civil war began in 2014, while a Saudi-led alliance has fought them for over ten years in support of the government based in Aden. A truce lasted for years before it broke down this summer. In September the Houthis pushed north along the Red Sea coast, seizing the port of Mokha and strategic islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

According to the BBC, the conflict, quiet for several years, flared again because of the wider Iran war. The truce reportedly unravelled after Saudi forces hit Sanaa airport to block an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Houthis answered by targeting Abha airport in Saudi Arabia and attacking Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

A market strike in Taiz province on Friday reportedly killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials. Each side has blamed the other for it. On Saturday the coalition said it had downed a Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh, while pro-government media reported that government troops had beaten back a Houthi assault at al-Aqroud in Taiz.
The UN puts the death toll since fighting intensified at more than 1,600, with over 300,000 people displaced. Houthi leader Mahdi al-Mashat has promised retaliation for the recent attacks.
items.cav: The casualty figures and the claim that Saudi Arabia carried out the strikes come from Houthi-run outlets and the Houthi health ministry, and the coalition has not responded. DW’s first headline gave a toll of 22 before it was changed to 33, so the count may still shift.
