items.op: When the only casualty figures come from one side of a war, the public is left to trust one party’s arithmetic. Civilian deaths, children among them, in al-Shariyah demand verifiable facts. The coalition should explain its targeting, and independent monitors should be allowed to investigate, before anyone is treated as settling the matter.

items.t: After the midterms, Republicans split over whether to stay with Trumpism or chart a new course
items.s: Republicans are taking stock after the 2026 midterms, which the BBC describes as the breakdown of the coalition that carried Donald Trump through three straight presidential nominations. The party now weighs whether to double down on Trump’s movement or look for a route beyond him.
p: Losses reached far beyond Washington. Republicans gave up control of the House and Senate, and also lost governorships and state legislatures, including in Texas and Kansas, states where Democrats had been locked out of power for decades. The BBC notes that the defeat quickly prompted questions about what the party looks like once Trump leaves the stage.

Responses on the right vary widely. Outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the midterms as a near-catastrophe for his party. Vice-President JD Vance placed much of the blame on public frustration with the war with Iran, argued that Republicans could still recover, and conceded that the aftermath would be contentious and internally divided.

The BBC’s Washington correspondent, Daniel Bush, frames the question as a choice between keeping Trumpism intact and charting a different path during Trump’s remaining time in office. Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC the party has to settle whether it revolves around one personality or around broader principles that can win in places beyond its strongest strongholds.

Hardliners who opposed Trump’s first campaign, often labelled “Never Trumpers”, want a return to the party’s pre-Trump traditions, pointing to the heavy election-night losses. The BBC argues that such a reversal would be very hard to achieve. Most Republicans have moved right on immigration and turned away from the interventionist foreign policy associated with George W Bush. Moderates in Congress have nearly vanished, and longtime critics of Trump such as John Cornyn and Susan Collins lost their seats this year.

Three days after the vote, Trump named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, succeeding Susie Wiles. According to the BBC, the appointment suggested Trump does not intend to soften his agenda. Steve Bannon, a key figure behind the Maga movement, warned of a “civil war” inside the party. He attributed the setback to the economy and overseas conflicts, argued that the Maga agenda had never been fully carried out, and urged Trump to press harder on mass deportations.

Other Republican strategists read the result as a warning. Whit Ayres said many Maga supporters remain loyal, yet a non-Maga segment of the party now makes up the majority. The BBC cites a New York Times analysis of voter data showing Latino support for Democratic candidates climbing 29 percentage points between 2024 and 2026, and backing from voters aged 18 to 29 rising 33 points.

Democrats also gained from a widespread belief that the Trump family and administration are marked by self-dealing and corruption. Trump’s attention to the White House ballroom and other Washington building projects, the BBC reports, reinforced the impression that he cared more about his legacy than about rising living costs. Benjamin Shrader, who leads the Young Republicans in Austin, said his party had been nearly swept aside in Texas by a Democratic wave.
items.cav: The Latino and youth figures come from a New York Times analysis that the BBC cites second-hand, and the evidence does not show how much weight each factor carried. Vance’s explanation and Bannon’s claims are the speakers’ own views, not established findings.
items.op: The central question for Republicans is whether they will answer to voters or to a single man. Voters who doubt the Trump family’s conduct deserve transparent answers, not a loyalty contest. A party that reads a defeat as a verdict on one leader rather than on its own record is likely to repeat it.

items.t: Israel’s president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
items.s: Isaac Herzog has handed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first attempt at forming a coalition after the recent vote produced no majority for either major bloc. Eisenkot has four weeks to try.
p: Herzog told the country he would give Eisenkot the first opportunity to assemble a new government. The decision followed a round of consultations with the parties after the vote left neither Eisenkot’s camp nor the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a working majority in the legislature.

The clock is now running. Eisenkot has 28 days to attempt the task, and the period can be extended by a further two weeks. Writing on X, the former military chief framed the moment as a call for a “national emergency government” and pledged to do all he could to meet that standard.

The arithmetic explains the stalemate. According to the BBC, Netanyahu’s Likud, together with its far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners, took 53 of the 120 seats. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition groups in his bloc took 48. The two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, won 19 seats between them, a record for Arab parties that the BBC linked to a jump in Arab voter turnout.

That result makes the Arab parties potential kingmakers, yet nearly every Jewish party had said before the vote that it would not join a government with them. Herzog’s office reported that incoming lawmakers recommended Eisenkot for the premiership 67 times and Netanyahu 46 times. The president is not bound to pick the leader of the largest party, and he has wide latitude to choose whoever he judges most likely to build a coalition.

The results point to three possible routes. One is a national unity government including both men. Another is a right-wing coalition drawing defectors from Eisenkot’s bloc. The third is an Eisenkot-led government propped up by the Arab parties. Speculation has grown that such a deal could be struck, although Eisenkot and all but one member of his bloc have previously ruled out serving with Arab parties. A deal with the ultra-Orthodox parties is also conceivable but would be hard to reach.

Israel has a precedent for power-sharing. In 2020, after three inconclusive elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed to rotate the premiership between them. Herzog, for his part, urged the factions to accept that in present conditions “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled”, arguing this would avoid another election. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel went to the polls five times.
items.cav: The reports do not say whether any party will reverse its pledge not to work with the Arab parties, so that route remains speculative. The seat counts and recommendation figures are as reported by the BBC and the president’s office, and the 2020 precedent is background rather than a forecast.
items.op: Herzog’s choice of Eisenkot, based on the publicly released tally of 67 to 46, is a defensible use of presidential discretion, and open reporting of that tally matters. The real test is whether the parties put stable governance ahead of their public vows. Voters who turned out in record numbers, Arab citizens included, deserve a government that does not treat their votes as untouchable.

items.t: Gloomy New Zealand voters deliver tightest election in years as major parties lose ground
items.s: New Zealand has elected a new government amid widespread gloom, with record numbers of voters abandoning the two major parties. The result leaves no clear mandate, and the smaller parties could hold the balance of power.
p: New Zealand voted in a new government on Saturday, with fog hanging over the capital, Wellington. According to the BBC, the mood among voters was as grey as the weather. Several people interviewed described apathy and dread. One 21-year-old, Imogen Vlutger, called the national mood “pretty flat”, and one man in his 40s said he had not voted at all.

Polling cited by the BBC suggests the sentiment is widespread. More than half of the country no longer sees New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a recent study that the BBC does not name, and a similar share fears the future will be worse. Many people told the broadcaster that the economy is struggling, jobs are scarce, and living costs have risen sharply.

The election itself reflected that frustration. A record number of voters deserted the two major parties, leaving neither with a clear mandate. Gains went to the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party. The Opportunity Party had never held a seat in parliament before, but it now has seven, which could give it the balance of power. Its leader, Quilae Wong, said voters had chosen to change New Zealand politics, and the party says it is willing to work with either major party.
It may be weeks before it is clear who will form the governing coalition and what deals have been made to do so. The BBC reports that the next prime minister will face a long list of problems.

Economists and researchers have described a country that was once known for its quality of life. University of Auckland professor Robert MacCulloch, a specialist in happiness economics, told the BBC that the lifestyle was good and that people could get by comfortably, even if they were not the highest paid.

The BBC describes a sharper decline in recent years, which many people linked to the Covid pandemic. Unemployment is at an 11-year high and still rising. For people under 24, the BBC reports, one in three either cannot find enough work or has none. Zainab Ali, chief executive of the support service Youth Inspire, said demand has never been higher, with waiting lists for its employment workshops running into the hundreds.

Healthcare and cost-of-living pressures were also cited. Household electricity bills have jumped, and the BBC reports that about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because of grocery prices, which it attributes partly to a supermarket duopoly. The article also points to a death in July of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait.
items.cav: The article does not say which parties will form the government, and the coalition talks are still unresolved. The study on national optimism and the polling are not named, and the BBC itself notes that the Wellington voters it spoke to may not be representative. Details of the emergency department death beyond the wait and the collapse are not given.
items.op: Disillusion with politics is not a reason to disengage; it is a reason to demand openness. Whoever builds the next coalition should publish the deals that bring it together. Voters who feel ignored are owed clear answers, including on how a man could wait nine hours in an emergency department.

items.t: Paraguay’s former president Santiago Peña charged over bank collapse links
items.s: Prosecutors have charged Paraguay’s former president, Santiago Peña, over his alleged business ties to a collapsed online bank. Peña denies wrongdoing, and the case has sparked protests across the country.
p: Paraguayan prosecutors have charged Santiago Peña, who was removed from office by the Senate, over his alleged links to Ueno Bank. The bank’s collapse left a large share of the population unable to reach their money, according to the reports.

Peña had offered to resign, but lawmakers, including members of his own party, voted to impeach him instead. Under the reports, that move stripped him of the immunity that ex-presidents usually enjoy. Impeachment charges alleged conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, the diversion of pension funds and a cover-up involving the central bank.

Prosecutors accuse him of breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain. According to a second report, he is also accused of steering government deposits to Ueno Bank and downplaying its financial problems despite warnings. He is further accused of a conflict of interest over the appointment of a former Ueno director to lead the central bank. He is reported to have held shares in the holding company until last year.

Peña’s lawyer, Ricardo Preda, called the allegations a “reckless accusation” and said that in Paraguay a minister, not the president, decides where state money is deposited. A judge ordered Peña held in pre-trial custody and froze the assets of Peña and a co-accused, Carlos Carvallo, who faces the same charges plus falsifying government documents.

The central bank says it has begun repaying Ueno customers and that more than half have recovered their funds. The BBC estimates about three million depositors still cannot access savings and pensions. Thousands protested in Asunción and elsewhere, and earlier clashes saw police use tear gas and water cannons. Vice President Pedro Alliana has been sworn in as interim president and promised compensation for those affected. Some demonstrators objected that he comes from the same party as Peña.

Senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of dereliction of duty, a finding made by lawmakers rather than a court. Peña, in a video posted on X, said it was never his intention to betray public trust.
items.cav: The reports differ on timing: the BBC says Peña was arrested on Friday, while the second report says he was charged and taken into custody on Saturday. Figures also vary, with the BBC citing about three million unable to access savings and the second report describing accounts held by nearly half of 6.5 million people. The “guilty” finding came from the Senate during impeachment, not a court, and the defence disputes all the charges.
items.op: Peña is entitled to a presumption of innocence and a fair trial, and the charges remain untested. Still, the stripping of immunity and the frozen assets show that accountability is being pursued through the courts. Paraguayans deserve full transparency about who approved those deposits and why warnings were ignored.

items.t: Six killed and more than a dozen hurt in Kraków shooting, police say
items.s: A gunman opened fire from a moving car in the main square of Kraków, Poland, killing six people and injuring more than a dozen, according to local authorities. The suspect was shot by police and detained, and no motive has been announced.
p: Police began receiving reports at around 3 p.m. local time that someone in a car was shooting at random people entering the city’s main square, a major tourist destination, a police spokesperson said. The gunman fired from the vehicle near Słowacki Street, according to local reports, before officers confronted him near the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets.

Police said the man was wearing military-style attire and used military-type firearms. During the arrest, officers opened fire, and the man returned fire, leaving two police officers among the injured. Authorities said more weapons had been secured in his car. The suspect, who is also in hospital, has not been named by officials.

Initial reports gave a death toll of five. The regional Małopolska government later said the number of people killed had risen to six, and the Małopolskie region governor, Krzysztof Jan Kleczar, told Polsat News that 12 of the injured were in a life-threatening condition.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “all circumstances” of the attack were being investigated and travelled to the city. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said he was in contact with the interior minister, the voivode and the emergency services. President Karol Nawrocki said he expected a full explanation of the circumstances.

Police said the suspect was Polish and rebuked conspiracy theories circulating on social media. Onet, citing police, reported that the man had no identification documents on him and that his identity was established through operational work.

A man who gave his name as Konrad and said he witnessed the shooting told the news website Interia that he saw shots fired from the driver’s side window. He ran to a police station on the main square and found people lying on the floor inside. His account has not been independently verified.

The US ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose, described the shooting on X as a mass attack and expressed solidarity with the city. No motive has been announced, and the sources do not say whether the suspect acted alone.
items.cav: Sources disagree on the death toll: one report cites five dead, while the regional government later said six. Several details, including the account of the witness and the description of the weapons, are second-hand or based on early police statements. The motive remains unknown.
items.op: Attacks on crowded public spaces demand patient, transparent answers rather than speculation. Poland’s promise of a full explanation must be kept in public view, with a verified timeline that residents and the families of the victims can trust. Rebutting online conspiracy theories is only a start; the state owes the city clear facts as the investigation proceeds.

items.t: Italian foreign minister says hackers published his personal data on the dark web
items.s: Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says criminal groups have been releasing his private information and targeting his relatives. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has blamed pro-Russian hackers.
p: Tajani wrote on X that, over several days, “cyber-criminals” had posted his personal details on the dark web while asking for more information about him. He argued that this put him at risk of new dangers and attempts to frighten him, though he did not describe what those dangers involved.

According to Tajani, the people behind the campaign are also going after his family. He connected the episode to Italy’s backing for Ukraine, saying that defending a sovereign state’s freedom and independence has made him a target for groups he called criminal.

Meloni publicly stood by Tajani and placed the blame on pro-Russian hackers. In a statement, she voiced serious worry about the trade in confidential material concerning government representatives and said it needed to be confronted firmly.
Meloni also flagged manipulated pictures that she said had been passed around by opposition members. She gave no information about what those pictures depicted.

Tajani did not say which kinds of information had been exposed. He indicated that the threat had not ended. He also raised the possibility that the attacks were a response to Rome’s work to shore up the digital protections of the Foreign Ministry, a point reported by Al Jazeera.

Tajani said his ministry was treating the matter seriously and was working with allied governments on a response. Al Jazeera also placed the affair in the context of a series of hoax bomb warnings across Europe, which have led to rerouted flights, alerts at broadcasters and sabotage of supermarket cooling equipment. Those sources do not tie these events to the data leak.
BBC News notes that Italy has supplied both humanitarian and military aid to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion.
items.cav: The sources do not identify the hackers beyond Meloni’s attribution to pro-Russian actors, and they do not say what data was published or what the threats involved. Tajani’s link to Ukraine policy and the alleged opposition-shared images rest on his and Meloni’s own statements, without independent detail.
items.op: A minister who says he is being intimidated over a political stance deserves a clear public account of what was exposed and who is responsible. If Rome wants to be trusted on security, it should share enough detail for independent scrutiny, not only condemnation.

items.t: Shooting in Krakow’s main market square leaves at least six dead and wounded, police say
items.s: At least six people were killed and about fifteen injured after a gunman opened fire from a car in the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on Saturday, according to police. The suspected shooter was wounded in an exchange of fire with officers.
p: Police in Krakow, Poland’s second-largest city, said a man drove into the main market square at around 3 pm local time, which is 1400 GMT, and began shooting at people from inside the vehicle. Early reports from the scene varied. One broadcast account, drawing on Reuters, cited at least five dead, while DW reported at least six killed and fifteen injured, with the toll rising in later updates.

Police said the gunman was reportedly a Polish citizen who acted alone. Officers shot him, and he was being taken to hospital, according to the force’s statement on X. Among the wounded are police officers, DW reported.

Authorities initially urged people in the immediate vicinity to move to a safe place. Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that police were investigating the attack and described it as “tragic”. President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, the wounded and their families.

Krakow lies about 250 kilometres from Warsaw and has more than 800,000 residents. It is a popular tourist destination, known for the main square, Wawel Castle and the cathedral on Wawel Hill. Al Jazeera’s brief report gave a figure of five dead and at least ten injured.
Reports say mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. Motive has not been stated in the material available so far, and the accounts of casualty numbers have not yet been reconciled.
items.cav: The death and injury tolls differ between outlets, and the figures were still being updated when the reports were filed. The gunman’s motive and any wider background are not described in the sources, and the nationality claim is reported rather than confirmed.
items.op: When a gunman fires at random people in a public square, the public needs a clear and timely account of what happened and why. Polish authorities should publish verified casualty figures and the findings of their investigation, so that public trust is not left to rumour.

items.t: New Zealand election leaves no clear winner as coalition talks loom
items.s: Preliminary results from New Zealand's weekend election point to a deeply divided parliament, with neither major bloc holding a clear path to government. Official confirmation is not expected until late November.
p: There was no clear winner after New Zealand’s general election on Saturday, and the leaders of the two major parties are preparing for negotiations on forming a coalition government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s centre-right National Party won 42 seats, the most of any party, according to preliminary results. That was still 19 short of the simple majority needed to govern. Its coalition partners, ACT and New Zealand First, would give the right-leaning side a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, did not concede. He said the “shape of the next government” would remain uncertain “for a while”. The Greens were projected to win 16 seats, ACT 13, New Zealand First 12, the Opportunity Party 7 and Te Pāti Māori 5.

The campaign was shaped largely by the cost of living and unemployment. More than 99 per cent of votes had been counted by the time of reporting, with National and Labour close on vote share. The two major parties together took around 60 per cent, which the BBC described as historically low support.

Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a “very hard-fought race” and said he would lead a caretaker government until final results are confirmed. The electoral commission is not due to announce the official result until 27 November. Hipkins said the next parliament would require all sides to compromise.

The Opportunity Party, a centrist group, crossed the 5 per cent threshold to enter parliament for the first time. Its leader, Qiulae Wong, said it would work with either side, though it would first negotiate with the party that wins the most seats. The BBC described it as this election’s kingmaker.

Election law expert Andrew Geddis of the University of Otago said special votes, including overseas votes, would need to be processed over the next three weeks, and that the outcome could hinge on very fine margins in individual electorates. New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional system makes coalition governments the norm.
items.cav: The source spells the Labour leader’s name inconsistently and gives only preliminary figures, so seat totals could change once special votes are counted. The claim that the Opportunity Party is a kingmaker is a description by the BBC and expert commentary, not a settled outcome.
items.op: Coalition talks should wait for every vote to be counted and certified, and the commission’s timetable must be respected. Voters deserve transparent results before any deal is struck behind closed doors. The next government will only be legitimate if its making is open to scrutiny.

items.t: Six killed and 15 injured in Kraków Main Square shooting, Polish authorities say
items.s: At least six people were killed and fifteen injured after a gunman opened fire on the main square of the Polish city of Kraków, according to authorities. The suspected gunman was shot by officers and taken to hospital.
p: The regional government of Małopolska confirmed the casualty figures on Saturday evening. Among the injured were two police officers, one with a gunshot wound and another in very serious condition after three gunshot wounds, who was undergoing surgery, according to police.

A spokesperson for the local firefighters told Polsat News that the attacker fired from a passing car. Police said the gunman is a Polish citizen and denied reports that a second perpetrator was being sought.

Numerous police cars and ambulances gathered near St Mary’s Basilica, and a helicopter from the air ambulance service was dispatched to the site. The city office said rescue services were working on the Main Square while police carried out operations in several locations.

President Karol Nawrocki said he was “deeply concerned” by the events and that the head of the National Security Bureau was travelling to Kraków. The story is still developing, and further details are expected as they emerge.
items.cav: The sources do not state a motive. The account of the shooting from a passing car comes from a firefighters’ spokesperson speaking to Polsat News, so it is second-hand. The municipal government and regional authorities gave differing sources for the initial information, and the death toll is described as “at least” six.
items.op: A mass shooting in a city centre demands full, prompt disclosure of what happened and why. Officials should clarify the suspect’s circumstances and the police response, so that public trust rests on verifiable facts rather than rumour.

items.t: National Trust members back a tender for a new bank with stronger environmental standards
items.s: Members of the National Trust have voted by a wide margin to seek a new banking partner, a decision aimed at the charity’s ties to Barclays. The trustees have backed the move, though the ballot does not bind them.
p: At its annual general meeting on Saturday, the charity approved a resolution directing it to launch a competitive tender for its banking arrangements. The trustees supported the resolution, according to the Guardian’s report.

For the first time, the tender would make a demonstrable environmental record a condition for any incoming bank, with a focus on protecting wildlife and cutting emissions. Campaigners counted 53,256 votes in favour and 4,094 against, and argued that charities should hold their lenders to the same green standards they apply to investments and suppliers.

Not everyone sees the result as a decisive shift. Some sources said the tender is unlikely to start for at least a year, a timeline the report attributes to insiders rather than to the charity itself.

Sandy Nairne, the board’s deputy chair, told members that the ballot offers trustees a useful gauge of opinion but does not oblige them to act. He said the board would weigh the outcome together with the debate held at the meeting before deciding its next steps.

Drew James, who proposed the resolution and belongs to Christian Climate Action, described the result as a sign of growing pressure on non-governmental organisations to justify their partners. Supporters contend that keeping Barclays as bank sits badly with the trust’s public warnings about climate change and nature loss, and with its statutory purpose under the National Trust Act 1907.

Barclays defended its position, saying it was honoured to bank the charity and pointing to more than $300bn (£225bn) of sustainable and transition finance mobilised over three years. Campaigners question how much that total matters, noting that the bank’s latest annual report indicates fossil fuel firms can draw on the fund so long as the money is not earmarked for oil and gas work directly.

The trustees have also made clear that the tender will not be limited to specialist ethical lenders. In their view, none of those institutions currently offers the cash handling, lending capacity and payments infrastructure a body of the trust’s scale requires, so the major UK clearing banks must remain eligible.

Restore Trust, a members’ group, said the vote pulls the charity away from its central job of looking after historic buildings and countryside. Its chair, Cornelia van der Poll, made that criticism publicly.
items.cav: The timing of the tender rests on unnamed insiders, and the report does not confirm when it will begin. The account relies on campaigners’ figures and on statements from Barclays and the trust, which have not been checked independently.
items.op: A charity that urges the public to bank ethically should be prepared to meet that standard itself. The trustees have the final word, and they should publish clear criteria and a timetable, so members can see whether their vote carries weight beyond a signal.
